The ocean already absorbs about a quarter of the CO2 emitted by humanity
Hello. This is the third installment of this series.
Last time, I wrote about the difference between CO2 "reduction" and "removal." This time, I will talk about the "ocean" itself, which I am looking to for help.
In fact, the ocean is already absorbing a massive amount of CO2, even without us doing anything. I would like you to know that fact, and its cost, first.
More than 10 billion tons of CO2 dissolve into the ocean every year
There is an estimate called the "Global Carbon Budget" that researchers around the world compile every year. It is like a household account book that tracks where the CO2 emitted by humans has gone.

According to the 2025 edition, CO2 emissions from human activities are approximately 42 billion tons per year. Of that, it is estimated that about 11 to 12 billion tons per year are absorbed by the ocean.

Surfing Diary 52nd Session: January Ocean and Thoughts on Physical Strength
It has been a while since my last session. I went to the ocean for the first time this year, about three weeks since my last visit. (I am a surfer over the age of 60.)

On a weekday in the third week of January 2026, I headed to my usual local surf spot. Although it was warm for January, the waves were small, and I surfed at the left side of the break where the waves were barely breaking.
The size was knee-high, with occasional waist-high sets. The wind was a light offshore breeze. I wore a semi-dry wetsuit, along with boots and gloves.

Perhaps because the waves were small, there were few people, and I was able to enjoy surfing at a leisurely pace. While waiting for waves out in the lineup, I happened to look down and saw that the water was clear enough to see the seabed. I realize that surfing always makes me feel relaxed and free.

The seawater is quite cold, but thanks to my full gear including gloves, I didn't feel the cold while in the water. However, that seems to have been an illusion, as the cold water was gradually draining my energy. After getting out of the water, changing, and sitting in the car seat, I felt a level of fatigue I don't experience in warmer seasons. Because of this, I took a short nap in the car befo

These changes in how I feel fatigue might be one of the signs of aging. However, I accept it as a phenomenon, and I plan to keep my midwinter surf sessions as short as possible and take longer breaks on the way home. That is how I hope to continue surfing for a long time to come.
